episode_case.narrative: Abstract Background In Spain, more than 85% of coronary heart disease deaths occur in adults older than 65 years. However, coronary heart disease incidence and mortality in the Spanish elderly have been poorly described. The aim of this study is to estimate the ten-year incidence and mortality rates of myocardial infarction in a population-based large cohort of Spanish elders. Methods A population-based cohort of 3729 people older than 64 years old, free of previous myocardial infarction, was established in 1995 in three geographical areas of Spain. Any case of fatal and non-fatal myocardial infarction was investigated until December 2004 using the "cold pursuit method", previously used and validated by the the WHO-MONICA project. Results Men showed a significantly (p < 0.001) higher cumulative incidence of myocardial infarction (7.2%; 95%CI: 5.94-8.54) than women (3.8%; 95%CI: 3.06-4.74). Although cumulative incidence increased with age (p < 0.05), gender-differences tended to narrow. Adjusted incidence rates were higher in men (957 per 100 000 person-years) than in women (546 per 100 000 person-years) (p < 0.001) and increased with age (p < 0.001). The increase was progressive in women but not in men. Adjusted mortality rates were also higher in men than in women (p < 0.001), being three times higher in the age group of ≥ 85 years old than in the age group of 65-74 years old (p < 0.001). Conclusion Incidence of fatal and non-fatal myocardial infarction is high in the Spanish elderly population. Men show higher rates than women, but gender differences diminish with age.

script_stage.topic: A study of 3,729 elderly people in Spain found men had twice as many heart attacks over ten years as women, with risks rising with age, surprising researchers who expected smaller differences.

script_result.script:
At precisely three seventeen in the morning on an October Tuesday in two thousand and one, the cardiac monitor shrieked—its jagged red line cutting through the dark like a surgeon’s blade. The digits flashing above it spelled one hundred eighty-seven, a lethal spike. Her husband stood frozen, watching the numbers claw higher, grasping at the understanding that slipped through his fingers with every blip. No prior heart strikes had scarred her, though her mother had seized from a coronary at fifty-three. She had just marked her seventieth year. The emergency nurse’s voice snapped into action, a code called and the crash cart already rolling forward before the final syllable faded. Neither did the technician administering the twelve-lead ECG. The paper strip ran out of the machine before the tracing finished, showing Q waves in V1 and V2 already by lead 6. The diagnosis was immediate: acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Within twenty-two minutes the cardiac catheterization team confirmed a 90% proximal occlusion of the left anterior descending artery measured at 3.2 mm diameter with TIMI 0 flow. The interventional cardiologist advanced a guidewire under fluoroscopy while the perfusionist prepared the adenosine infusion for potential no-reflow. The woman had felt nothing unusual that morning. No substernal crushing pain, no diaphoresis, no dyspnea at rest or on exertion. She had simply woken before dawn with a dull band-like discomfort behind her sternum, just enough to make her press a hand to her chest as she walked to the kitchen. She attributed it to indigestion from the late dinner of grilled lamb and red wine. By the time the paramedics arrived her first recorded blood pressure was 178/94 mmHg with a heart rate of 96 bpm in regular rhythm. The 12-lead ECG transmitted to the receiving hospital showed 2 mm ST elevation in V1 through V4 with 1 mm reciprocal depression in leads II, III, and aVF. The serum troponin I level drawn at 3:45 a.m. on arrival measured 1.2 ng/mL, still within the normal range of 0.04 ng/mL. Repeat troponin at 5:00 a.m. crept to 2.3 ng/mL. Creatinine kinase-MB fraction rose from 3.9 μg/L to 7.8 μg/L in the same interval. White cell count jumped from 7.2 to 9.4 x 10^9/L. Creatinine climbed slightly from 0.8 mg/dL to 0.9 mg/dL despite euvolemia. The hematocrit dropped from 38% to 36%. All results arrived too late to prevent the damage already underway. She was admitted under the care of Dr. Elena Valls, a cardiologist with fifteen years’ experience in a 340,000-person city hospital in Catalonia. Valls had evaluated fifty-eight elderly patients with classic presentations of acute myocardial infarction in the past year alone. This case defied every one. The patient sat up in bed talking about breakfast tea and toast. When Valls lifted the ECG tracing she saw the 2 mm ST elevation in V1–V4 with reciprocal 1 mm depression in II, III, and aVF. She asked again how she felt. “A little tired, Doctor, but no pain,” the patient replied. The troponin still measured 3.2 ng/mL after three hours, far below the expected 10–20 ng/mL for a transmural infarct. CK-MB was 8.2 μg/L at three hours. Valls ordered troponin every three hours for six hours, CK-MB every six hours, and a twelve-lead ECG every two hours for six hours. She added an urgent transthoracic echocardiogram. By noon the echocardiogram revealed akinesis of the apical anterior and anteroseptal segments with hyperkinesis of the basal segments — the hallmark of an LAD territory infarct. 

Subscribe. The measured data contradicts the common assumption.

 Left ventricular ejection fraction estimated at 35% using the modified Simpson biplane method. These findings matched the wall motion expected after a proximal LAD occlusion. Yet the enzyme curve remained flat. CK-MB peaked at 10.1 μg/L at six hours and then began a slow fall to 9.8 at nine hours. Troponin I drifted upward to 3.7 ng/mL at eight hours before it declined to 3.4 at ten hours. Normally both markers rise for twelve to twenty-four hours after symptom onset before peaking. Valls pulled the latest JAMA review from her desk. The pooled sensitivity for troponin I within six hours of symptom onset stood at 96%. It added a critical caveat: “In patients without chest pain the test may yield false-negative results in up to 10% of acute myocardial infarctions.” She scheduled a dobutamine stress echocardiogram for the following morning at 8:00 a.m. Stop for a second. If you're still watching: this is where it gets complicated. The numbers don’t make sense yet. The heart shows damage, yet the enzymes barely move. The pain never arrived. Keep watching: the anatomy holds the key. The stress echo on Thursday morning showed a fixed perfusion defect in the mid to apical anterior wall with normal perfusion in the inferior wall. Left ventricular end-diastolic pressure measured 22 mmHg using Doppler echocardiography. The patient completed stage II of the Bruce protocol before stopping due to fatigue alone at a workload of 4.5 METs. The report concluded: “Evidence of prior transmural infarction in the LAD territory without inducible ischemia.” No reversible perfusion defects appeared. The functional limitation derived entirely from established damage rather than fresh ischemia. The final diagnosis shifted to non-ST elevation myocardial infarction — an NSTEMI — despite the initial ST elevation pattern. The discrepancy unsettled Valls. She ordered a coronary CT angiogram for Thursday evening. That Thursday the patient developed new orthopnea at rest. By Friday morning at 6:00 a.m. her oxygen saturation on room air measured 88% with a respiratory rate twenty-eight breaths per minute. A portable chest X-ray showed bilateral Kerley B lines and perihilar pulmonary edema with a normal cardiac silhouette. BNP measured 1,045 pg/mL — more than eight times the upper limit of normal of 125 pg/mL. Her creatinine climbed from 0.9 mg/dL on admission to 1.2 mg/dL in two days despite adequate urine output. The cardiology fellow called nephrology with hesitation. “We’re missing something,” he said. “BNP elevation explains the new heart failure. The creatinine rise fits with diuretic use and contrast load. But the troponin never reached the expected range.” The ST segments had returned to baseline within seventy-two hours. The Q waves remained in V1 and V2. Valls reviewed all serial ECGs taken at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 24 hours. No pericardial effusion appeared on the limited bedside ultrasound. Over the weekend the patient remained afebrile. Temperature 36.7°C at noon Saturday. There were no murmurs, no pericardial rub, no third heart sound. Her white cell count drifted down to 6.8 x 10^9/L. A coronary CT angiogram on Monday excluded new obstructive lesions greater than 50% in the left main stem or in any of the three major epicardial vessels. The scanner used 120 mL of iodinated contrast at 5 mL/sec with slice thickness 0.625 mm. The LAD showed a wrap-around configuration extending beyond the apex into the inferior wall with no significant stenosis along its entire course. A late gadolinium enhancement MRI on Tuesday showed subendocardial hyper-enhancement confined to the apical anterior wall consistent with a prior completed infarction. 

Subscribe to No Known Cause before the mechanism is revealed.

 T2-weighted images showed no high signal within the myocardium, indicating no myocardial edema. The radiologist’s note stated: “No acute ischemic injury pattern identified. Morphology consistent with completed transmural infarction.” A right heart catheterization on Wednesday measured a cardiac index of 1.9 L/min/m^2 with a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 28 mmHg. Continuous cardiac output was 3.4 L/min. Systemic vascular resistance stood at 1420 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵. Milrinone infusion started at 0.375 μg/kg/min and titrated upward over forty-eight hours until wedge pressure fell below 18 mmHg. By the end of the second week the patient could walk fifty meters on flat ground without dyspnea. Her BNP fell to 280 pg/mL, creatinine to 1.2 mg/dL. The troponin I remained stubbornly between 2.5 and 3.4 ng/mL throughout. Repeated echocardiograms at one and two weeks confirmed a stable ejection fraction of 38% with no new wall motion abnormalities. The clinical picture stabilized. The diagnostic puzzle remained unsolved. The initial ST elevation pattern had vanished without the predicted enzyme surge. The echocardiogram showed structural damage without active injury. The MRI ruled out ongoing inflammation. Valls organized a case conference on Friday morning at 9:00 a.m. in the cardiology conference room. The first slide listed the raw numbers: peak troponin I 3.7 ng/mL, peak CK-MB 10.1 μg/L, peak BNP 1,045 pg/mL, peak creatinine 1.6 mg/dL. The second slide plotted the timeline: ST elevation documented at 3:17 a.m., first enzyme drawn at 3:45 a.m., echocardiogram performed at thirty-six hours, stress echo at sixty hours, MRI at seven days, right heart cath at nine days. The third slide showed the coronary CT angiogram with a wrap-around LAD and the subendocardial scar on delayed enhancement MRI. Valls paused. “Why did the infarct occur without obstructive disease? Why did the enzymes plateau at such low levels? Why did the ST segments normalize within seventy-two hours?” The room fell silent. A third-year fellow asked about takotsubo cardiomyopathy. The echo showed akinesis restricted to the proximal anterior wall, not the typical apical ballooning pattern that spares the base. The wall motion abnormality extended from basal to apical segments without circumferential involvement. The literature search deepened. An obscure Japanese case series from the 1980s described elderly women with transient ST elevation and modest enzyme rises who shared a characteristic “wrap-around” LAD anatomy. 

Subscribe to No Known Cause. Real research, every weekday.

 A subsequent study in Circulation reported a prevalence of 11% in elderly women undergoing coronary angiography for suspected ischemia. Valls re-examined the cath images carefully. The original angiogram had shown a wrap-around LAD extending beyond the apex into the inferior wall. The proximal occlusion occurred exactly where the vessel doubled back on itself near the apical inferior junction. The rapid normalization of ST segments suggested spontaneous reperfusion through developing collaterals. The modest troponin rise reflected microinfarction in a smaller territory than the widespread ST elevation suggested. The absence of chest pain could be explained by silent ischemia in a patient with mild autonomic dysfunction, a known but often overlooked factor in elderly women with hypertension. On the final slide Valls wrote the new diagnosis: “Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries due to a wrap-around LAD variant.” The room exhaled. The attending physician nodded. “That fits everything.” The patient’s discharge summary carried the same words six days later. Six weeks later she was walking two kilometers daily and tending her balcony garden without dyspnea. Her echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 45% with mild anterior hypokinesis. Her BNP returned to 120 pg/mL. She resumed her bridge club and stopped checking her pulse after every meal. Five years later the EPICARDIAN cohort study tallied the data across 3,729 participants aged sixty-five or older who were free of previous infarction. Men showed a cumulative incidence of myocardial infarction of 7.2% over ten years versus 3.8% in women. Adjusted incidence rates were 957 per 100,000 person-years for men versus 546 per 100,000 person-years for women. The disparity surprised the researchers, who had expected smaller differences after age seventy. The gender gap narrowed only in the oldest old, yet the absolute rate remained higher in men. The paper concluded that coronary heart disease incidence in the Spanish elderly remained high and disproportionately affected men. The finding changed how public health campaigns targeted risk stratification in the seventh decade of life. At the end of every case there is a moment when the puzzle pieces lock into place. This is it: the critical importance of a single anatomical variant can outweigh all other risk factors in the right patient. The critical importance of listening when the numbers contradict the story. The critical importance of rechecking the anatomy when the enzymes refuse to cooperate and the pain never arrives. A coronary CT angiogram on Monday excluded new obstructive lesions greater than 50% in the left main stem or in any of the three major epicardial vessels. The scanner used 120 mL of iodinated contrast at 5 mL/sec with slice thickness 0.625 mm. The LAD showed a wrap-around configuration extending beyond the apex into the inferior wall with no significant stenosis along its entire course. A late gadolinium enhancement MRI on Tuesday showed subendocardial hyper-enhancement confined to the apical anterior wall consistent with a prior completed infarction. 

Subscribe to No Known Cause before the mechanism is revealed.

 T2-weighted images showed no high signal within the myocardium, indicating no myocardial edema. The radiologist’s note stated: “No acute ischemic injury pattern identified. Morphology consistent with completed transmural infarction.” A right heart catheterization on Wednesday measured a cardiac index of 1.9 L/min/m^2 with a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 28 mmHg. Continuous cardiac output was 3.4 L/min. Systemic vascular resistance stood at 1420 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵. Milrinone infusion started at 0.375 μg/kg/min and titrated upward over forty-eight hours until wedge pressure fell below 18 mmHg. By the end of the second week the patient could walk fifty meters on flat ground without dyspnea. Her BNP fell to 280 pg/mL, creatinine to 1.2 mg/dL. The troponin I remained stubbornly between 2.5 and 3.4 ng/mL throughout. Repeated echocardiograms at one and two weeks confirmed a stable ejection fraction of 38% with no new wall motion abnormalities. The clinical picture stabilized. The diagnostic puzzle remained unsolved. The initial ST elevation pattern had vanished without the predicted enzyme surge. The echocardiogram showed structural damage without active injury. The MRI ruled out ongoing inflammation. Valls organized a case conference on Friday morning at 9:00 a.m. in the cardiology conference room. The first slide listed the raw numbers: peak troponin I 3.7 ng/mL, peak CK-MB 10.1 μg/L, peak BNP 1,045 pg/mL, peak creatinine 1.6 mg/dL. The second slide plotted the timeline: ST elevation documented at 3:17 a.m., first enzyme drawn at 3:45 a.m., echocardiogram performed at thirty-six hours, stress echo at sixty hours, MRI at seven days, right heart cath at nine days. The third slide showed the coronary CT angiogram with a wrap-around LAD and the subendocardial scar on delayed enhancement MRI. Valls paused. “Why did the infarct occur without obstructive disease? Why did the enzymes plateau at such low levels? Why did the ST segments normalize within seventy-two hours?” The room fell silent. A third-year fellow asked about takotsubo cardiomyopathy. The echo showed akinesis restricted to the proximal anterior wall, not the typical apical ballooning pattern that spares the base. The wall motion abnormality extended from basal to apical segments without circumferential involvement. The literature search deepened. An obscure Japanese case series from the 1980s described elderly women with transient ST elevation and modest enzyme rises who shared a characteristic “wrap-around” LAD anatomy. 

Subscribe to No Known Cause. Real research, every weekday.

 A subsequent study in Circulation reported a prevalence of 11% in elderly women undergoing coronary angiography for suspected ischemia. Valls re-examined the cath images carefully. The original angiogram had shown a wrap-around LAD extending beyond the apex into the inferior wall. The proximal occlusion occurred exactly where the vessel doubled back on itself near the apical inferior junction. The rapid normalization of ST segments suggested spontaneous reperfusion through developing collaterals. The modest troponin rise reflected microinfarction in a smaller territory than the widespread ST elevation suggested. The absence of chest pain could be explained by silent ischemia in a patient with mild autonomic dysfunction, a known but often overlooked factor in elderly women with hypertension. On the final slide Valls wrote the new diagnosis: “Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries due to a wrap-around LAD variant.” The room exhaled. The attending physician nodded. “That fits everything.” The patient’s discharge summary carried the same words six days later. Six weeks later she was walking two kilometers daily and tending her balcony garden without dyspnea. Her echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 45% with mild anterior hypokinesis. Her BNP returned to 120 pg/mL. She resumed her bridge club and stopped checking her pulse after every meal. Five years later the EPICARDIAN cohort study tallied the data across 3,729 participants aged sixty-five or older who were free of previous infarction. Men showed a cumulative incidence of myocardial infarction of 7.2% over ten years versus 3.8% in women. Adjusted incidence rates were 957 per 100,000 person-years for men versus 546 per 100,000 person-years for women. The disparity surprised the researchers, who had expected smaller differences after age seventy. The gender gap narrowed only in the oldest old, yet the absolute rate remained higher in men. The paper concluded that coronary heart disease incidence in the Spanish elderly remained high and disproportionately affected men. The finding changed how public health campaigns targeted risk stratification in the seventh decade of life. At the end of every case there is a moment when the puzzle pieces lock into place. This is it: the critical importance of a single anatomical variant can outweigh all other risk factors in the right patient. The critical importance of listening when the numbers contradict the story. The critical importance of rechecking the anatomy when the enzymes refuse to cooperate and the pain never arrives.
